articles.title: How do I choose the right gemstone?
articles.metaDescription: Birth stones, durability, and practical questions to ask before you buy a gemstone — with modern Kolkata-fusion styling from Pradeep Jewellers.
articles.intro: The right stone balances tradition, daily wear, and your budget. Use this guide to narrow choices before you visit the counter — so every rupee goes toward a piece you will actually wear.

sections.heading: Start with purpose, not trend
paragraphs: Astrological guidance is meaningful for many families, but the stone must still suit how you live. A soft stone in a heavy daily ring will scratch and chip; a durable stone in a occasional pendant may never show its beauty.
Ask yourself: Is this for daily wear, festivals only, or a once-in-a-lifetime bridal set? That answer changes which gems are realistic.

sections.heading: Durability matters on the hand
paragraphs: On the Mohs scale, rubies and sapphires (corundum) score 9 — excellent for rings. Emeralds are softer and often oiled; treat them gently and avoid ultrasonic cleaning at home.
For heavy use, favour stones with fewer internal fissures. A slightly smaller, cleaner stone often outlasts a large included one.

sections.heading: Colour and origin
paragraphs: Two rubies of the same carat can differ sharply in price because of hue, saturation, and clarity. Burmese pigeon-blood tones command premiums; well-cut Thai or African stones can look superb at gentler prices.
Always view stones in natural daylight and warm indoor light — showroom LEDs can flatter or flatten colour.

sections.heading: Questions to ask your jeweller
paragraphs: Is the stone natural, heated, or treated? Is it accompanied by a lab certificate? What is the recommended setting — prong, bezel, or closed back?
At Pradeep Jewellers we weigh every gemstone before setting and document treatments on your bill so there are no surprises later.

takeaways: Match the stone to how often you will wear the piece.
Prefer durability (corundum) for rings you never take off.
Compare colour in daylight, not only under shop lights.
Ask about treatment, certificate, and setting style in writing.

articles.title: What are the 4Cs of diamonds?
articles.metaDescription: Cut, colour, clarity, and carat explained — how to read a diamond certificate before you buy.
articles.intro: The 4Cs — Cut, Colour, Clarity, and Carat — are the global language jewellers use to describe diamonds. Understanding them helps you compare quotes fairly and spot where to invest or save.

sections.heading: Cut — the sparkle engine
paragraphs: Cut is not the shape (round, oval, pear) but how well facets interact with light. An excellent cut can make a slightly smaller stone look larger and brighter.
Poor cut leaks light through the pavilion; the stone looks dull even with high colour and clarity grades.

sections.heading: Colour — the D to Z scale
paragraphs: D is colourless; Z shows noticeable yellow or brown. For 18K yellow gold settings, G–I often looks icy because the metal warms the overall appearance.
In white gold or platinum, many buyers target F–H for a crisp look without paying for top-tier D–E unless size is secondary.

sections.heading: Clarity — eye-clean is the goal
paragraphs: Grades run from Flawless (FL) to Included (I). Most jewellery uses VS or SI stones that appear clean to the naked eye.
Inspect under 10× magnification in-store. A tiny inclusion under a prong may be acceptable; one dead centre in the table is not.

sections.heading: Carat — weight vs spread
paragraphs: Carat is weight, not face-up size. A well-spread 0.90 ct can look larger than a deep 1.00 ct with a small diameter.
Prices jump at milestone weights (0.50, 0.70, 1.00 ct). Slightly under a milestone can free budget for better cut or colour.

sections.heading: Reading your certificate
paragraphs: IGI, GIA, and similar reports list the 4Cs plus fluorescence, measurements, and proportions. Match the laser inscription on the girdle to the report number when possible.
Keep the certificate with your purchase invoice — it protects resale value and insurance claims.

takeaways: Prioritise cut for brightness before chasing top colour alone.
Choose colour grade to suit your metal (yellow vs white).
Eye-clean SI or VS is enough for most finger sizes.
Compare spread and cut quality, not carat alone.

articles.title: Which ring size will fit perfectly?
articles.metaDescription: Measure ring size at home, when to resize, and why half-sizes matter for comfort.
articles.intro: A ring that spins or pinches will stay in the drawer. Sizing is quick when you measure correctly — especially for surprise gifts and international finger standards.

sections.heading: Measure when fingers are normal
paragraphs: Fingers swell in heat and shrink in cold. Measure in the evening at room temperature for the most reliable fit.
If you are between sizes, go half a size up for wide bands; narrow bands can sit true to size.

sections.heading: At-home methods
paragraphs: Wrap a strip of paper around the knuckle you want the ring to pass over, mark the overlap, and measure the length in millimetres. Match to an Indian/British size chart.
Borrow a ring that already fits the same finger and measure its inner diameter with a ruler — more accurate than guessing from shoe size.

sections.heading: Surprise gifts
paragraphs: Trace an existing ring on paper or press it into clay. Your jeweller can estimate size within a quarter size.
For solitaires, slightly loose is safer than tight — resizing down is easier than stretching thin shanks.

sections.heading: When to resize
paragraphs: Plain gold bands resize cleanly. Full-eternity diamond bands often cannot be sized much without disturbing the line of stones.
If weight fluctuates seasonally, consider a comfort-fit band or a sizing insert for occasional wear.

takeaways: Measure in the evening at room temperature.
Wide bands usually need a half size up.
Use an existing ring or mm chart — not guesswork.
Eternity bands need correct size at purchase.

articles.title: How is sterling silver (925) tested?
articles.metaDescription: Hallmarks, simple tests, and how to spot plated silver so you buy genuine 925 sterling.
articles.intro: Sterling silver is 92.5% pure silver alloyed for strength. Plated brass and nickel silver are often sold as “silver colour.” Know the checks so your invoice matches the metal you receive.

sections.heading: What 925 means
paragraphs: The stamp 925 (or Sterling) means 925 parts per thousand silver, usually with copper for hardness. Fine silver (.999) is softer and rare in everyday jewellery.
Indian BIS hallmarking for silver articles helps verify purity when present on the piece.

sections.heading: Hallmarks and invoices
paragraphs: Look for 925 on an inconspicuous spot — inside shanks, on clasps, or earring posts. Match the description on your bill: “sterling silver 925” not just “silver colour.”
Reputable sellers state weight in grams and purity on the invoice.

sections.heading: Simple checks at home
paragraphs: Sterling tarnishes to a yellow-brown patina; many platings peel or show a different colour at worn edges.
A strong magnet test: sterling is not magnetic; steel cores in fakes may stick. This is indicative, not definitive — use a jeweller’s acid or XRF test for certainty.

sections.heading: Care and longevity
paragraphs: Store in anti-tarnish pouches, avoid chlorine and perfume contact, and polish with a soft cloth — not abrasive toothpaste on oxidised finishes.
Rhodium-plated silver stays bright longer; when replating is needed, ask whether the base metal is verified 925 first.

takeaways: 925 means 92.5% silver — confirm on piece and invoice.
BIS hallmark adds confidence when available.
Magnet and wear-edge checks screen obvious fakes.
Proper storage slows tarnish on genuine sterling.
